subject: biology
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {level} {subject} question on {lo}, then mark my answer against the mark scheme.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for {board} {level} {subject} simply, with a clear example and the most common mistake students make.

questions.q: In the co-transport of glucose in the ileum, glucose is absorbed into the epithelial cell because:
options: glucose is pumped directly by ATP into the cell
a sodium-glucose co-transporter carries glucose in alongside Na+ moving down its gradient
glucose is actively pumped out of the cell
glucose diffuses freely through the phospholipid bilayer
questions.explain: Na+ entering down its gradient (maintained by the Na+/K+ pump) drives glucose into the cell against its gradient via the co-transporter.

questions.q: A coenzyme differs from a prosthetic group in that a coenzyme:
options: is a permanently bound metal ion
is part of the protein's primary structure
is a small organic molecule that binds temporarily and is often derived from vitamins
is an inorganic cofactor
questions.explain: Coenzymes are loosely bound organic molecules, frequently vitamin-derived, that participate transiently, unlike permanently bound prosthetic groups.

questions.q: When the difference in concentration of a freely diffusing molecule across a membrane is doubled, the rate of simple diffusion will:
options: approximately double, because rate is proportional to the concentration gradient
stop
halve
stay the same
questions.explain: For simple diffusion across a membrane, rate is proportional to the steepness of the concentration gradient, so doubling the gradient roughly doubles the rate.

questions.q: Vmax represents:
options: the maximum rate of reaction when all active sites are saturated with substrate
the optimum temperature for the enzyme
the rate of reaction at zero substrate
the substrate concentration at which the enzyme denatures
questions.explain: Vmax is the theoretical maximum rate achieved when enzyme active sites are fully saturated and working at capacity.

questions.q: A competitive inhibitor reduces the rate of an enzyme-catalysed reaction by:
options: increasing the Vmax of the reaction
binding away from the active site and changing the active site shape
binding to the active site, having a similar shape to the substrate
permanently denaturing the enzyme
questions.explain: A competitive inhibitor has a complementary shape to the active site and competes with substrate for it; its effect is overcome by raising substrate concentration.

questions.q: A polysaccharide gives a positive iodine test (blue-black) and on complete hydrolysis yields only alpha-glucose, including some from 1,6 bonds. The molecule is most likely:
options: amylose only
cellulose
chitin
amylopectin
questions.explain: Amylopectin stains blue-black with iodine and is a branched chain of alpha-glucose with both 1,4 and 1,6 glycosidic bonds.

questions.q: Enzymes increase the rate of reaction by:
options: raising the temperature of the substrate
increasing the activation energy of the reaction
lowering the activation energy by providing an alternative reaction pathway
being permanently changed by the reaction
questions.explain: Enzymes lower the activation energy required, allowing more substrate molecules to react at a given temperature.

questions.q: In which stage of mitosis do chromosomes align along the equator (metaphase plate)?
options: Telophase
Prophase
Metaphase
Anaphase
questions.explain: During metaphase, chromosomes line up at the cell equator attached to spindle fibres by their centromeres.

questions.q: Cell fractionation to isolate organelles requires the tissue to be placed in a solution that is cold, buffered and isotonic. The solution must be isotonic to:
options: prevent organelles bursting or shrinking due to osmotic water movement
speed up respiration
denature enzymes that might digest organelles
maintain a low pH
questions.explain: An isotonic solution has the same water potential as the organelles, preventing osmotic gain or loss of water that would damage them.

questions.q: A non-competitive inhibitor that binds reversibly to an allosteric site will, on a rate-against-substrate graph, produce:
options: an unchanged Km but a reduced Vmax
no change to either value
a reduced Km and unchanged Vmax
an increased Vmax
questions.explain: Because substrate binding is unaffected, Km stays the same, but fewer functional enzymes mean a lower maximum rate, so Vmax falls.

questions.q: Hydrogen bonding between water molecules arises because water is:
options: a non-polar molecule with even charge distribution
a polar molecule with a partially negative oxygen and partially positive hydrogens
an ionic compound that dissociates fully
a hydrophobic solvent
questions.explain: Unequal sharing of electrons makes oxygen slightly negative and hydrogens slightly positive, allowing hydrogen bonds between adjacent water molecules.

questions.q: Why is starch an effective storage molecule in plants but unsuitable as the main respiratory substrate transported in solution?
options: It is too small to store energy
It cannot be hydrolysed to glucose
It is insoluble and compact so it does not affect water potential, but this also makes it unsuitable for transport
It is highly soluble and so leaks out of cells
questions.explain: Starch's insolubility means it has no osmotic effect and stores compactly, but the same property makes it unsuitable for transport, where soluble sucrose is used instead.

questions.q: The sodium-potassium pump in co-transport maintains a low intracellular Na+ concentration by:
options: pumping glucose out of the cell
allowing Na+ to diffuse passively out
breaking down the cell membrane
actively pumping 3 Na+ out and 2 K+ in using ATP
questions.explain: The Na+/K+ ATPase actively exports 3 Na+ and imports 2 K+ per ATP, creating the Na+ gradient that powers glucose co-transport.

questions.q: A phospholipid differs from a triglyceride in that a phospholipid has:
options: one fatty acid replaced by a phosphate-containing hydrophilic group
three fatty acids attached to glycerol
no glycerol backbone
only ester bonds and no hydrophilic region
questions.explain: In a phospholipid, one of the three fatty acids of a triglyceride is replaced by a hydrophilic phosphate group, making the molecule amphipathic.

questions.q: A red blood cell placed in pure water bursts (haemolysis) because:
options: solutes enter the cell by active transport
water leaves the cell by osmosis
the membrane actively pumps water in
water enters down a water potential gradient and the cell has no rigid wall to resist swelling
questions.explain: Pure water has a higher water potential than the cytoplasm, so water enters by osmosis; lacking a cell wall, the animal cell swells and lyses.

questions.q: Cholesterol contributes to membrane stability at low temperatures by:
options: increasing active transport
forming hydrophilic channels
preventing the phospholipids from packing too closely, so the membrane does not become too rigid and stays fluid
allowing phospholipids to pack tightly and freeze solid
questions.explain: At low temperatures cholesterol stops phospholipids packing tightly together, maintaining fluidity and preventing the membrane becoming too rigid.

questions.q: The function of the rough endoplasmic reticulum (RER) is to:
options: digest worn-out organelles
synthesise and transport lipids
produce ATP through respiration
synthesise proteins via attached ribosomes and transport them
questions.explain: The RER is studded with ribosomes that synthesise proteins, which are folded and transported through its cisternae.

questions.q: A plant cell at full turgor has a pressure potential of +600 kPa and a solute potential of -800 kPa. Its water potential is:
options: -200 kPa
+200 kPa
questions.explain: Psi = solute potential + pressure potential = -800 + 600 = -200 kPa.

questions.q: Compared with a saturated fatty acid, an unsaturated fatty acid:
options: is more hydrophilic due to extra hydroxyl groups
contains no carbon-carbon double bonds and is solid at room temperature
has a longer hydrocarbon chain by definition
contains one or more C=C double bonds causing kinks, lowering the melting point
questions.explain: C=C double bonds introduce kinks that prevent close packing of chains, so unsaturated lipids have lower melting points and tend to be liquid.

questions.q: Two enzymes catalyse the same reaction; enzyme X has a lower Km and a lower Vmax than enzyme Y. This means enzyme X:
options: binds substrate more readily but has a lower maximum rate when saturated
requires no substrate to function
is denatured
binds substrate less readily but works faster when saturated
questions.explain: A lower Km means higher affinity (binds substrate at low concentration), while a lower Vmax means a slower maximum rate once saturated.

questions.q: When an enzyme is immobilised by entrapment in alginate beads, the rate of reaction may be slightly lower than for free enzyme because:
options: the enzyme denatures instantly
the optimum temperature falls to 0 C
no enzyme-substrate complexes can form
the substrate must diffuse into the bead to reach the active sites, slowing the reaction
questions.explain: Entrapment can hinder substrate access as it must diffuse through the matrix, though immobilisation still allows reuse and greater stability.

questions.q: A change in pH away from the optimum reduces enzyme activity because:
options: it increases the kinetic energy of the substrate
H+ or OH- ions disrupt ionic and hydrogen bonds, altering active site shape
it permanently increases enzyme concentration
it lowers the activation energy
questions.explain: Changes in pH alter charges on R-groups and disrupt bonds maintaining the tertiary structure, distorting the active site.

questions.q: Why does an enzyme show specificity for a particular substrate?
options: because the precise 3D shape of the active site, determined by tertiary structure, is complementary to one substrate
because the enzyme provides activation energy to all molecules equally
because the substrate has the same primary structure as the enzyme
because all enzymes catalyse every reaction
questions.explain: The active site's specific shape, arising from the protein's folding, is complementary only to a particular substrate, conferring specificity.

questions.q: End-product inhibition, a form of metabolic control, typically operates because the end product acts as a:
options: non-competitive (allosteric) inhibitor of an enzyme earlier in the pathway
competitive inhibitor of the final enzyme
substrate for the first reaction
coenzyme for the first enzyme
questions.explain: The end product binds allosterically to an early enzyme, reducing its activity and preventing wasteful overproduction; this is negative feedback.

questions.q: The total magnification of a light microscope using a x10 eyepiece and a x40 objective lens is:
options: x4
questions.explain: Total magnification is the product of the eyepiece and objective magnifications: 10 multiplied by 40 = 400.

questions.q: A cell measures 30 mm in a photomicrograph taken at a magnification of x1500. The actual size of the cell is:
options: 2000 micrometres
20 micrometres
0.02 micrometres
45 micrometres
questions.explain: Actual size = image size / magnification = 30 mm / 1500 = 0.02 mm = 20 micrometres.

questions.q: Why does a high density of mitochondria near a cell-surface membrane suggest the cell carries out a lot of active transport?
options: mitochondria increase membrane fluidity
mitochondria store the absorbed glucose
mitochondria supply the ATP required to power carrier proteins against the concentration gradient
mitochondria act as channel proteins
questions.explain: Active transport needs ATP, so many mitochondria close to the membrane indicate a high demand for energy to drive pumping.

questions.q: A scanning electron microscope (SEM) is particularly useful for studying the surface of a pollen grain because it:
options: passes electrons through a thin section to show internal detail
uses visible light to give true colour
scans the surface and detects reflected/secondary electrons to build a 3D image of surface topography
requires a living, hydrated specimen
questions.explain: An SEM scans the specimen surface, and detected secondary electrons produce a three-dimensional image of surface features.

questions.q: A non-competitive inhibitor acts by:
options: binding to an allosteric site away from the active site, altering the active site shape
increasing substrate affinity
being outcompeted by high substrate concentration
binding to the active site and blocking substrate entry
questions.explain: Non-competitive inhibitors bind at a site other than the active site, changing the enzyme's tertiary structure so substrate can no longer bind effectively.

questions.q: Why can small non-polar molecules such as oxygen and carbon dioxide cross the membrane by simple diffusion?
options: They are actively transported
They are small and non-polar, so they dissolve in and pass through the hydrophobic phospholipid bilayer
They require carrier proteins
They are repelled by the hydrophobic core
questions.explain: Being small and non-polar, these molecules dissolve in the lipid bilayer and diffuse directly across down their gradient.
